title: The fifth taste
text: Ask most people how many basic tastes there are, and they will probably name four: sweet, salty, sour and bitter. For a long time, scientists in Europe would have given the same answer. Yet there is a fifth taste that you experience almost every day, whether you are eating a slice of pizza, a bowl of soup or a plate of chips with ketchup. It is called umami, and the story of how it was discovered begins in a kitchen in Japan more than a century ago.

In 1907, a chemist called Kikunae Ikeda was having dinner at home in Tokyo when he noticed something about the soup his wife had made. It was dashi, a traditional Japanese stock prepared with a type of seaweed called kombu. The soup had a rich, savoury flavour that did not seem to fit into any of the four known categories. Ikeda was so intrigued that he decided to investigate it in his laboratory.

After months of experiments, he managed to isolate the substance responsible for the flavour. It was glutamate, a natural compound found in many foods. Ikeda named the taste umami, from a Japanese word that means something like delicious, and in 1908 he published his findings. Being a practical man, he also developed a way to produce glutamate in the form of a white powder that could be added to food. It went on sale the following year and became extremely popular in Asian cooking.

Outside Japan, however, many scientists remained unconvinced. For most of the twentieth century, umami was often dismissed as simply a combination of the other tastes. It was not until the early two thousands that researchers identified specific receptors on the tongue that react to glutamate. This discovery finally proved that umami is a separate basic taste, and Ikeda, who had died decades earlier, was shown to have been right all along.

Once you know what umami is, you start to notice it everywhere. Ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, cheese such as parmesan, cured ham and soy sauce are all rich in glutamate. In fact, many classic dishes from around the world combine several of these ingredients, which may explain why they are so satisfying. Some researchers have even suggested that we are born with a liking for umami, since human breast milk contains a high level of glutamate.

Chefs have also learnt to use umami to their advantage. A little of it can make food taste fuller and more balanced, which means that less salt is needed. For this reason, some nutritionists believe umami could help people reduce the amount of salt in their diet, especially older people who may have lost some of their sense of taste.

So the next time you take a bite of a cheese and tomato sandwich and think it tastes good, you will know why. Thanks to one curious scientist and a bowl of soup, we now understand that our tongues are a little more complex than we once believed.
